results.title: GPU Cloud Pricing Explained: On-Demand, Reserved, Bare Metal
highlights:
October 21, 2026

GPU cloud pricing looks simple on a rate card, but the hourly number hides two separate decisions: How you commit to paying for capacity, and how much of the server you actually get. Understanding both is what separates a GPU bill that tracks useful work from one that pays for idle hardware.

- On-demand buys flexibility: You pay per GPU-hour with no commitment and can stop at any time, which suits experiments, bursty jobs, and workloads whose utilization you have not measured yet.
- Reserved pricing buys a lower rate: Committing to a term lowers the effective hourly price, but you pay for every hour of the term, so it only saves money when utilization stays above the break-even point set by the discount.
- Bare metal is a deployment model, not a billing term: It gives you the whole physical server with root access and no hypervisor, which can be bought on demand or reserved, and NVIDIA has measured virtualized training running 12% slower than bare metal.
- Published rates are only a starting point: On GMI Cloud, on-demand rates start at $2.60 per GPU-hour for H100, $3.20 for H200, $5.00 for B200, and $8.00 for GB200 as of October 2026, while committed plans are discounted and storage and networking are priced separately.
- Utilization decides which model wins: Cast AI’s 2026 analysis of production clusters found average enterprise GPU utilization of roughly 5%, which shows how easily reserved capacity turns into paid idle time. Matching the pricing model to measured usage is the single biggest lever on GPU cost.

...

On-demand pricing charges a rate per GPU-hour while your instance is running, with no minimum term. You can start, scale, and stop whenever you like, and the bill follows usage, provided you actually release capacity when it is idle. Metering granularity matters for short jobs. Some providers bill by the second or minute, others round up to the hour, and that difference adds up quickly for bursty work.

On GMI Cloud, all GPU resources are dedicated, single-tenant instances priced per GPU-hour, with the rate depending on GPU type and deployment model. Pay-as-you-go containers have no expiration date and can be terminated at any time, and pay-as-you-go managed clusters are charged by the minute with no upfront cost, as GMI explains in its guide to comparing container, bare metal, and managed cluster quotes.

...

On-demand pricing wins whenever the workload is short, bursty, or not yet measured. That covers prototyping, benchmarking a new model, one-off fine-tuning runs, evaluation jobs, and inference traffic whose daily pattern you have not seen yet. It is also the right way to start almost any new project, because a few weeks of on-demand usage turns a utilization guess into a measured number before you commit to anything.

results.title: Comparing Managed B200, B300, and NVL72 Quotes With Different Delivery and Commitment Terms
results.author: Colin Mo
highlights:
November 01, 2026

Two quotes at the same hourly rate produce different totals once billing starts at different events, one at contract signature and the other when your team can run jobs. Compare managed Blackwell quotes on one project timeline instead of on rate: place each delivery window against your need-by date, count the GPU-hours each minimum commitment obliges you to pay for, price the interim capacity a late delivery would force you to buy, and record what each provider actually guarantees. On GMI Cloud today, the Blackwell lineup (B200, B300, GB200 NVL72, GB300 NVL72) is taken as pre-orders while H100 and H200 can be run immediately, and our pricing covers both on-demand use and committed structures, so our sales team can price a Blackwell pre-order and the H100 or H200 capacity that would run before it side by side.

...

## Blackwell pre-order and the capacity that bridges to it

Our Blackwell lineup is in pre-order, and commitment options for it are set with our sales team. Reserved capacity and sustained deployments lower unit GPU cost. H100 and H200 are available now on dedicated, single-tenant GPUs, which is the interim capacity in the method above.

Managed GPU Cluster (early access) is requested through the console and reviewed by GMI support before resources are provisioned, as the GPU Compute documentation describes. A cluster can run on per-minute pay-as-you-go billing or on a prepaid plan, and growing an existing cluster is a Node Request.

If part of the commitment is for serving, Prime Inference has no minimum contract: on-demand billing is hourly per GPU, reserved capacity is available on a seasonal or annual basis at lower per-hour rates, and B300 is one of its hardware options. Qualified prospects receive free GPU-hour trial credits, so model performance can be measured on your own workload before you pick a term.

results.title: Lambda announces GPU price rises of about 15% — B200, H100 and A100 80GB, from Nov 16 | GPUJournal
highlights:
# Lambda announces GPU price rises of about 15% — B200, H100 and A100 80GB, from Nov 16

Nov 6, 2026

Read on Lambda's own pricing page today, Nov 6, 2026: the Instances table now prints the prices that take effect on Nov 16, 2026 — HGX B200 up $1.00 an hour, H100 up $0.60 and A100 80GB up $0.40. It is the largest single announced rise we have caught this autumn, and renters have ten days' notice.

Image: GPUJournal price record — read on lambda.ai/pricing

What was announced, in the pricing page's own words (read Nov 6, 2026): 'These prices take effect November 16, 2026, at 00:00 UTC. Until then, log in to your Lambda Cloud account to see current pricing.' The printed Nov 16 rates: HGX B200 $7.69 an hour (from the $6.69 last verified on Nov 5, +14.9%), HGX H100 $4.59 (from $3.99, +15.0%), HGX A100 80GB $3.19 (from $2.79, +14.3%), and HGX A100 40GB unchanged at $1.99. Lambda is also now at a new address — lambda.com — announced on its blog on Nov 5, 2026; the pricing page itself still answers at lambda.ai/pricing.

How we are treating it: an announced rise is not a live price. Our board keeps Lambda's last verified rates until Nov 16 and will move only when the new rates are re-verified in effect on or after that date — the rise is recorded in Price Watch today as announced, with both dates. One consequence of the announcement is already live, though: Lambda's currently-effective rates can no longer be read on its public page, only after logging in, so today's public check could verify the future rates but not re-read the current ones.

What it does to the board when it lands: Lambda's B200 at $6.69 is currently the cheapest verified HGX B200 instance rate we list from a self-serve cloud; at $7.69 it would sit above RunPod Community's $5.98 marketplace rate and just below RunPod Secure's $7.99. Its H100 at $4.59 would remain above the board's best H100 SXM offer (TensorDock, from $2.25 at an 8-GPU minimum) but move Lambda from the middle of the H100 pack toward its top. Around-the-clock, the announced rises add about $730 a month per B200, $438 per H100 and $292 per A100 80GB on a 730-hour month.

Every month we check the public on-demand prices of specialist GPU clouds to set our own: CoreGPU prices every GPU at least 25% below the market median. This is the data behind that number, as listed on November 4, 2026.

## Method

- One on-demand price per provider and GPU, taken from public pricing pages or price APIs. Prices for 8-GPU nodes are divided by eight.
- Specialist GPU clouds only for the median. Hyperscalers (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Oracle) are listed separately because their prices are 2.5 to 4.5 times higher.

results.title: Nebius removes its spot-price ceiling — preemptible GPUs can now cost more than on-demand | GPUJournal
highlights:
Nov 2, 2026

In an update note dated Nov 2, 2026 on its own blog, Nebius says the cap that kept its dynamic spot price one cent below the on-demand rate is gone. Spot still has a floor — it just no longer has a top, and setting your own max price is now the only brake.

...

What changed, from Nebius's own post “Introducing spot pricing for preemptible VMs” (published Sep 22, 2026; read Nov 2, 2026): its update note, dated Nov 2, 2026, reads — “this section previously stated that the spot price always stays between a floor and a ceiling one cent below the on-demand rate. We have removed the ceiling. Customers can cap what they pay by setting a max price.” The post's how-it-works section now states plainly: “There is no upper limit, so during periods of high demand the spot price can rise above the on-demand GPU-hour rate.”

How the mechanism works, in the same post: the spot price for a GPU type in a region is set from available capacity and real-time demand, recalculated up to every 15 minutes, and it still cannot fall below a set floor — only the ceiling has gone. A renter who sets a max price keeps the old protection by hand: when spot rises above the cap, the instance stops, data is retained, and it can restart when the price falls back — automatically for Kubernetes clusters, manually (or via Terraform, SDK, API or CLI) for standalone VMs. A renter who instead chose to follow the spot price has no cap at all after today's change.

What did not change: Nebius's on-demand list. Re-read on Nebius's own prices page on Nov 2, 2026, B300 is $9.50 an hour, B200 $8.50, H200 $5.40, H100 $4.50, RTX PRO 6000 $1.80 and L40S from $1.55 — every figure the same as our Nov 1 read. This is not a price rise in the list; it is the removal of the guarantee that the interruptible lane is always the cheaper one.
